104.s: They recommend Willie the Lion Smith's, Mingus's, Hampton Hawes's and Dizzy's autobiographies, Duke's Music Is My Mistress and Bill Crow's Jazz Anecdotes, saying a musician's own story is best.
104.q: Not like that. I just put these little pieces together. But then I read Duke’s book, which of course Stanley Dance wrote a very good deal of it. But Duke wrote some of it. He was a wonderful writer. There’s certain passages that you know that he was the one that wrote that particular passage.

104.t: Perfect pitch, poor reading and who reads well
104.s: She has perfect pitch but calls her reading terrible, and names Dick Hyman, Hank Jones, Fred Hersch and John Bunch as great readers.
104.ch: Dream band, reading and closing thoughts
104.q: Awful. It’s been that way for years. I’ve never been a good reader, because nobody had me learn piano. The only reason I can read at all is having taken violin lessons, which I didn’t want to take.

104.t: Regretting that she never learned to read well
104.s: She wishes she could read, recalling learning Grieg at the Guildhall by checking against a Rubinstein record, and says classical players are often poor readers too.
104.ch: Dream band, reading and closing thoughts
104.q: Gee, I’ve said enough already. But it’s funny. The reading thing. It’s a shame. If I had it to do all over again, I would like to read. I would like to be able to read. But I never bothered, because I could always pick something up. And then, pieces I was learning at the Guildhall, of course I had…

104.t: Learning to read music and winning festival improvisation categories
104.s: Violin and Miss Jarvis taught her to read; local festival pieces were by MacDowell, and she always won the improvisation category.
104.ch: Jazz records, vaudeville and starting out
104.q: Yes. I never was a really good reader, but because of studying the violin, I got to read the treble clef, and then . . . with the . . . I don’t know how I ever got to getting to the bass clef. I think that must have been her as well. And then there was this other person, Gwen Massey. I can’t seem…

385.t: How he learned to read: Mel Bay and classical piano books
385.s: He learned counting from a Mel Bay beginner book then classical piano books until he could read fairly well.
385.ch: Chords, recordings and his own groups
385.q: The system that I had, a lot of people don't wanna accept it. See, it was a long time before I even knew what I was doing myself. I knew that I was playing but I didn't know anything --- no music. But then I just took it up and got me

385.t: Not reading music: Tatum and Slam, and faking a symphony date in Germany
385.s: Nobody in the trio read music; he describes learning a score by ear at a rehearsal for Odetta in Germany and Tatum's perfect pitch.
385.ch: Three Deuces and 52nd Street with Tatum
385.q: Oh yeah. He didn't read music. Nobody read no music. We had no time for no music. I don't know if Slam could read or not, even. Maybe, I really don't know. I know I didn't. Shit, never crossed my mind to read no music. I have faked it quite a few times. I mean faked it too, I faked it in Germany…

385.t: Erroll Garner's speed and the fear of reading music
385.s: He talks about down strokes versus up and down picking and the belief that learning to read makes you mechanical, mentioning Miles Davis.
385.q: But Erroll Garner could play faster notes than I could play. He was a taught person. And it was a thing called the up and down stroke, which makes you produce the speed as far as playing, whereas I had mostly a down-- I had a wrist, like Montgomery had his thumb. All downstrokes, but eventually it…

385.t: Learning to read and writing the block-chord book
385.s: He taught himself to read from a small book, and his book puts a chord under every note, for piano, six-string and vibes.
385.ch: Chords, recordings and his own groups
385.q: ... No, the first time I ever thought about it must have been about '68 or '69. ... I say, "damn, everybody always ask me can I read this, can I read that. So I got no teacher, so I got a little old book. So I set myself up there with that book and count and one and two and three. See, the funny…

182.t: Early barber saxophonist; copying parts from piano covers
182.s: Tom cannot recall a barber who was an early saxophonist, then says the red books were the hardest and he copied parts with Louis Dumaine.
182.q: Well, I don't know if he lived up there or not, I forget. I'm not sure. He's a barber. He's one of the first saxophone players in. Well. Mmhm. Mmhm.

182.t: Being called a parlor musician who read music
182.s: He explains he learned by reading, not by ear, and other bands like Sam Morgan's and Chris Kelly's came to him for music.
182.q: You see I wasn't a head man so much. I see. You understand? I see the music, now if I see the music I play with it about two or three times, well I'd get the chorus. Then I'd have it. Then I'd have it. With the voice I couldn't get it, you understand? As long as I get it, play it two or three times…

182.t: Parlor music, reading and learning cornet from a method book
182.s: Tom explains that people wanted head music not notes, called him parlor music, and that knowing the divisions and scale let him teach himself cornet from a method book.
182.q: Well, right kind, just any little thing you hear. Yeah. Any little thing you hear, the other fellow play, you catch that. He wasn't playing no, he wasn't with the orchestration music, he wouldn't stand about that. You see? He used to call it parlor music. I used to go to play, there was a fish fry,…

190.t: Reading only in the Navy dance band
190.s: They discuss how the service bands allowed no faking, though solos were made up and learned numbers could be played without looking.
190.q: You had to read. No faking there. You had to read there. You could have a parade. But you couldn't think in the dance bands in the services. No, no. You only had to read there too. You could have everybody in a military band in a dance band. Some fellas couldn't know. They were very, very good on…

190.t: Old-time New Orleans players had to read
190.s: They remember good bass, banjo, clarinet and trumpet players in New Orleans and agree you could not join a band unless you read.
190.q: That's right. you heard these great musicians when you're younger. You think getting that sound in your ear when you're young helps too? Yeah. Yeah, man. Boy, had nothing but a good musician around there. This way you had to come for good bass players, trombone players, trumpet players, banjo…

190.t: Dejan at the Japanese Tea Garden, and a reading player
190.s: Dejan says he was hired at the Japanese Tea Garden despite weak reading and tells of a rival band playing next door, with a player who could only read.
190.q: Hold that door on the air. Always could read. That's all he could do, read. That fellow, boy, that fellow. Always could read. You buy that piece of music, that was it. That was it. Always could read. In the never band, you played baritone.

290.t: Reading music and carrying orchestrations to jobs
290.s: He was not a sight-reader but learned parts between tunes, and always brought orchestrations to jobs.
290.ch: Clubs, readers and musicians he knew
290.q: Well, no. Most all the bands you played with, there was more people who didn't read than with Red. There was only a few with Red, you know. And then with Red wasn't professional readers because I was one of them. You were? Oh, I wasn't professional. I couldn't read on site. You know, somebody gave…

290.t: Scott Joplin, favorite numbers and which musicians could read
290.s: Talk of Joplin orchestrations, Sonny Henry's reading, and bands like Piron's and Robichaux's that had readers.
290.ch: Clubs, readers and musicians he knew
290.q: Yeah. I play the love band. Yeah. He plays all those, Scott Joplin. Yeah, you have the band parts too, eh? Yeah, right. Yeah. Scott Joplin. Scott Joplin, yeah, that was.

290.t: Who got hired: readers, politics, and audiences hating music racks
290.s: Hiring turned on need and ability to read, though crowds disliked bands seen with sheet music.
290.q: Well, I know, I know that, but let's go back to this politics, political. I think the thing was being done like that, too, you know. You had to know somebody. Yeah. And if you didn't know nobody...

378.t: Reading music is a matter of confidence
378.s: Reading is just practice and confidence, and he credits Trumbauer in the Whiteman band for improving his reading.
378.q: And I'd be on trains and I'd study the harmony books, all these sorts of things. That's when I did it on the trains. Now the practical side of reading music I think that's quite -- people think that's hard.

378.t: Frankie Trumbauer teaches himself to read
378.s: Trumbauer did not read when Norvo first heard him on the boats, then locked himself away for months reading everything.
378.q: Cause I think I learned better to read, after Whiteman's band, for Frankie influenced me very much, Frankie Trumbauer, in reading.

378.t: Teaching himself to read, arrange and memorize
378.s: Apart from about ten lessons in Jacksonville he was self-taught; he explains how he learned clefs, memorized scores by sight and wanted to write.
378.q: Well, let me explain it this way. The way I got into writing, more or less, was when I started to play with four hammers, and it all goes in a number of years later (unintelligible), I'm getting ahead of myself --

418.t: Learning positions, reading and a first taste of arranging
418.s: A pianist-bandleader wrote slide positions over the notes to teach him to read; being fired suddenly stranded him and pushed him to write his own parts.
418.ch: Small groups, Europe and Kansas City memories (repeated passages)
418.q: So that way...I guess that halfway(?) / eventually(?) helped me to learn to read. Then I started doing it, writing(?) it off like that myself, on numbered... On pieces, I'd put the position, third, fourth or second... I would put a position, you know, over the note. So that way I... I think that's…

418.t: Learning positions, reading and a first taste of arranging
418.s: A bandleader who wrote slide positions over the notes helped him learn to read, and he began arranging his own parts after being fired.
418.ch: Early bands, Calloway to Basie and Kansas City (third typescript)
418.q: There's a guy that taught me where do was at and I later found out that it's the key of B flat. You know -- so, but at the time do, re, me, fa, sol, la, te, do. That's what he said -- you know.

418.t: Learning positions, reading and a first taste of arranging
418.s: A bandleader wrote slide positions over the notes to teach him to read; being fired suddenly pushed him to arrange his own parts.
418.ch: Small groups, Europe and Kansas City memories (repeated passages)
418.q: There's a guy that taught me where do was at and I later found out that it's the key of B flat. You know -- so, but at the time do, re, me, fa, sol, la, te, do. That's what he said -- you know.

259.t: Hospital aside and Buddy Christian faking reading
259.s: After an aside about his x-ray, he says Buddy Christian had girls play pieces, then caught the key by ear so everyone thought he could read.
259.ch: Early heroes and Kid Ory band
259.q: Yeah, did they give you an x-ray down there? Where down? Hospital. Oh yeah. Yeah. But they said they didn't find nothing down there. They said it wasn't the matter with my lungs. Well, they're talking about two months to find something on me. Yeah. They laid me all kinds of ways down there. Yeah.…

259.t: How Vincent learned to read music
259.s: He took lessons from several teachers, was helped by his brother and his blind father counting for him.
259.q: Named Pinn? Pinn, Pinn and uh. Oh Pinn? Pinn. Pinn. Pinn he couldn't read. He couldn't read or Lee. Yeah. Zeb kept by telling Buddy to read. Lee could spell a little bit Lee Cotty but maybe Lee was something like me you know. I always kept with musicians and learning more with him and learning…

816.t: Learning to read music and checking parts
816.s: Warner learned to read from the method book and had a reader check disputed parts; Kid Rena's men played partly by ear.
816.q: Yeah, I thought you were by the end. Start writing, writing, learning how to read, because I couldn't play a thing out of head, see? And whenever anybody contradict me, say I wasn't making something right, I went to this man here, see? And when I got in the room together, he said, well, go on over…

816.s: Allen reassures them about the tapes; Sonny Henry and Warner argue that a musician must both read and fake.
816.ch: Eureka Brass Band and Sonny Henry
816.q: You can play with fellas that can use you in those things. Me too. I like his playing. You go get with some other bands, like Up The Line. Now, you know when you go up the line, that routine's all right, but they want you to see too. Yeah. You can only say, I'm a trombone player, you see, and I can…

251.t: Reel four opens; musicians reading music for nightclub acts
251.s: Dick Allen announces the fourth reel. Albert resumes a fragment about musicians who could read music for nightclub performers.
251.q: Okay, we were talking about, you had to read the poems. The band, as I told you previously, the musicians in those days, they played music. There weren't too many Finnish musicians that had learned music. So when Tra would get these jobs in these nightclubs that required music to be played for the…

251.t: Head arrangements, stock arrangements and who read in Floyd's band
251.s: The band used many head arrangements and stocks; only a few could read, and Albert transposed parts from violin, clarinet or piano.
251.q: A lot of head arrangements and the piano player was a good reading musician, not a hell of a piano player, but a good reading musician. Then he had, well, Ben O'Kennedy, who was the trumpet player, was a seasoned musician. He was great. And I imagined through him and the piano player and the…

264.t: Reading bands: Robichaux and Manuel Perez
264.s: Robichaux's and Perez's bands read music.
264.q: Yeah, yeah, he was a great musician, yes he did. Yeah, everybody read it. Robichaux too, Manny Joan Robichaux, they were reading bands.

264.t: Whether Buddy Petit composed or read music
264.s: Petit wrote no tunes but could read a little and taught the band new numbers by ear; few in the band read.
264.ch: Technique and the Covington band's sound
264.q: No, Buddy never did worry about no music like that. But he could spell a little bit. Buddy could read a little bit. Yeah, but he never did worry about. Or make up any tunes. I mean even if they weren't written

2.t: Do the best jazz musicians read music?
2.s: Why the nonreading myth does not hold for Louis or Bunk, and Bunk's advice to start with solfege.
2.q: You'd have a hard time making that argument stick, though, too, with a person like Louis, who learned to read very well, I guess, in the 20s on the boat, and then even took lessons in Chicago. And, of course, Bunk always could probably read quite well ever since he started. In fact, that's the way…

2.t: Reading in ragtime and eastern bands
2.s: The reading versus aural-roots contrast, ragtime players like Chauvin and Turpin, and Bob Wright's ear.
2.q: Most of the ragtime players probably did read not all of them either. I think Chauvin didn't. I'm not sure if I ever heard that Tom Turpin did and there was a fellow that I recorded once Charlie Thompson who was quite a good ragtime player. He couldn't read but the tradition usually was I think…

601.t: Tom called 'parlor music' because he read but did not fake
601.s: Tom says players who could not read called him parlor music because he read well and could not fake. When music became popular, Isaiah Morgan, Chris Kelly and others came to him wanting to learn.
601.ch: Trombonists, old string bands and dance steps
601.q: Yeah. He noticed all, but he couldn't, he wasn't sure he could count, you know. Yeah. The division, you know. He didn't show he could count. He, he come out and eat with me. I've been him playing it about four times. Yeah. And I told him, I said, you can go. But after he played, I know some of them…

601.t: What the old string-band players did for work, and Tom learning rhythm from a method book
601.s: Tom and Russell discuss the day jobs of these musicians and how few bands there were. Tom describes how he learned to divide time with a dollar ABC method book, with Jimmy Palao's help.
601.ch: Trombonists, old string bands and dance steps
601.q: Did he have any other job or did he make his living in music? Well, I don't know. I don't know about any job. I know Ford used to play bass. I don't know what he used to do. I think he used to work at the slaughterhouse. Yeah, the slaughterhouse down at the barracks down there. Oh, yeah. Yeah. And…

279.t: Faking, reading music, and playing by ear
279.s: Hug explains 'fake', New Orleans non-readers, the stigma of not reading, and creativity from the ear.
279.q: Yeah, fake, yeah, fake was always a term that we used, because most of the New Orleans musicians were non-readers. You know, I mean, as Dick Allen knows, the old-time musicians like Papa Lane and, well, Shawky wasn't much of a reader.

279.t: Reading versus faking, and the Suburban Gardens story
279.s: A story of failing a written dance number at Suburban Gardens, and why musicians should read.
279.q: There were many names. But as you said before, Dick, I think that's a good thing to think about. While we're talking about these fellows, I don't know if you would say that they were all real jazz piano players. That is, in a real jazz sense. They may have been able to play with dance bands and…

285.s: He did not read well, bought a method book for fifty cents, and relied on his ear.
285.q: Well, I was going to ask in reading, when you first learned to play, you didn't really play. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

285.t: Theater pit versus dance band with Blossom Seeley
285.s: He learned from the piano with Seeley's act and contrasts hearing each other in a band with the spread-out pit.
285.q: Just like when with Celie now. She had a colored boy around New York by the name of Bill Beaudry. Bill Beaudry made all her arrangements. He made arrangements for the Ziegfeld, see? And the Dillingham shows. Bill Beaudry made her arrangements for her act. Other than the popular songs that were my…

633.t: Country bands versus city bands, reading and playing by ear
633.s: He thinks the country bands were better than bigger-name city bands, a view confirmed when he taught musicians in the WPA band.
633.q: Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. Well, we'd get together on that, you see. We'd get together on that and prices that and they're going to play it that way. Yeah. See now, I had a cousin playing trumpet with me. He was pretty good on making the mixture notes in there, you see. And I was pretty good too…

633.t: Frankie Dusen could not read music
633.s: Barnes doubts Dusen taught bands since he could not read, recalling him in the WPA band.
633.q: I wonder, too, somebody told me he couldn't read. I wonder how he could go around and teach a band. It's wrong, it's wrong. The last place I played with him, I don't know, I went in, of course we had a project band, we used to call it WPA band, you know? And he was in there when he was signed up…

879.t: Donald Miner's band, Second Liners and reading on jobs
879.s: Pickup band of Donald Miner, how little reading the rock jobs need, the six Second Liners, and concerts with June Gardner and James Black.
879.q: Well, these type of jobs, well I have no reason on it. It's strictly as what you know, card changes and so forth and so on. I listen to them and you know them. But it's fairly easy like I said, once you've been through it once before you know just how I go about it.

879.t: Reading, harmony and six years of study
879.s: He learned strictly by reading, wants to be an all-round musician, studied harmony on his own, and studied about six years with Corzell.
879.q: No, it was strictly reading. Uh, when I first started off with strictly reading music. Uh, this is how I got into the St. Augustine band. It's strictly reading. You have to know how to read. And, uh, right now I still read a little music, uh, these dance bands I play, these dance bands I play with.…

820.t: Third reel: managers and leaders of the Owls
820.s: The third reel begins and Frank explains Earl Crum managed the Owls, nobody led, and who could read.
820.q: Earl Crum was the manager. Leader? I don't think there was any leader. They just put the music out there on the stand and they went along and if they did any improvising they did it as a group to go along there, but they didn't read too well. You agree with me, Godfrey? Yeah. Sieg Christensen, when…

820.t: Reading ability in the Owls and when Pinky joined
820.s: Frank and the interviewer discuss who could read in the band, the Owls' breakup after the Edgewater, and Pinky joining after Frank did.
820.q: Yeah, he, you know those tuba players, as you well know, you know. You start to give them a violin sheet, you know, or something like that. It's kind of a little fast one. That's like Jumbo used to tell me. He looked at my part over there when he was playing some of those stuff over there. He says,…

127.t: Playing by ear and learning to read in the Army
127.s: He played by ear, then watched Lewis Mathis in the Army to learn to read.
127.q: By ear. That's when I'd whistle something up and pick the horn and blow it.

127.t: Brass bands in 1919 and who read music
127.s: Punch explains that the brass bands played marches by ear with few readers, and that he learned music from Joe Howard and Paul Roger.
127.ch: Musicians he knew and played with
127.q: No, they played more marches then. But I'm going to tell you now, I ain't going to lie to you. Hick was a very few men's in them bands reading. Like the trumpet players be reading. But them other guys were just speaking. I mean, you know, using their brains. They could hear a tune and play it.…

729.t: Making charts by ear and perfect relative pitch in Nashville and Muscle Shoals
729.s: Session players wrote their own number charts from the demo and needed relative pitch.
729.q: Well we do it by ear. You know you listen to the demo and I can remember going to play on sessions in Muscle Shoals and Nashville and Atlanta, and they wouldn’t even come in with the chart, even a number chart. They’d just play you the demo and you sat there with your own paper making your own…

729.t: Dionne Warwick catches a wrong chord; schooled vs self-taught; number charts
729.s: Warwick spots a half-step error in a chart; most pop stars were self-taught, and Eddie Gomez balks at a number chart.
729.q: I think so. I don’t know any singer I ever worked with — well no, I can tell you a couple. When I produced Dionne Warwick’s albums for Clive Davis, Dionne had gone, she was a a music teacher. And we were doing a session one day, it was a Michael McDonald song that must have had dozens of chord…

471.t: How Cobb learned to read music
471.s: He learned to read in Washington with his teacher and Rick Henderson's parts, and notes that Buddy Rich, Erroll Garner and Wes Montgomery did not read.
471.q: I learned how to read in Washington, with – I’m telling you, with being with the teacher, and with Rick. Rick had – he used to write little parts for the nine-piece band that we used to go play the things in the Colonnade with, and like that. So I learned how to read a little bit like that. When I…

471.t: Reading charts and house bandleaders in the theaters
471.s: Cobb says theater work required reading charts and a bandleader like Rick Henderson writing arrangements.
471.ch: Bird, Coltrane and Dinah Washington recollections
471.q: Yeah. You had to read charts and stuff like that. So you had to know all of that stuff. It was a good thing. It was a good learning process.

68.t: Playing in any key by ear, and learning to read
68.s: Tate says he played in any key before learning scales; reading is a handicap if lacking.
68.q: I just grabbed the horn and I -- no, I didn't. This was before I went into scales, see? It's only when I went into scales and things, that's when it kind of changed me down. It kind of slowed. Then you get a little conscious of what you do. I think it can kind of pull you back. It did me, I know it…

68.t: Bostic sight-reads the hard Oliver arrangements
68.s: Bostic plays a difficult part cold and outplays the band.
68.q: with us?" says, "75 dollars a week." He says, "How much?" So we says, "75 a week." He says, "I'll go." (Laughter.) Shit, he went home and he didn't have nothing but a toothbrush and maybe a couple shirts and things. He went on and carried them on down there. So now, after we go down there the next…

70.t: Shorty Baker learns to read in Redman's band
70.s: Redman found Harold Baker in St. Louis in 1936 and taught him to read; working with Redman was like school.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: And Shorty Baker, Harold Baker. I worked with him in Don Redman's band. In fact, we took him away from St. Louis in 1936. Don picked him up. He was a slow reader and Don taught him how to read. Like I told you, it was the same as going to school when you worked with Don.

70.t: Making up parts and learning from Redman and Edward Cuffy
70.s: With few second trombone parts he invents his own; Redman, who knew every instrument, taught him and Cuffy helped him practice.
70.q: So I sang, went on and sang with the band and I got so, just like we was speaking it before, I got so that I didn't have a lot of second trombone parts, you know.

120.t: Learning to read from Joe Hooven and alternating with Pollack
120.s: Hooven marks fingerings under the notes; Davison says the band was an education, and the band alternated monthly with Pollack's.
120.ch: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
120.q: Everything went outside unless, of course, it was raining or something - now, in the meantime, you know, Joe is teaching me how to read -- I mean a little more and a little more -- that's the slow way to learn---

120.t: Joe Rulo teaches him to read by position
120.s: Cornetist Joe Rulo shows him a quick sight-reading method in the locker room, and he comes to find classical parts easier than jazz.
120.ch: Benny Meroff and Chicago's jazz scene
120.q: Yeah but not good enough. And, so, Joe Rulo, who was the other cornet player in the band, said - look - if you want to really do yourself a favor -

234.t: Leonard Feather's Encyclopedia of Jazz and the need for first-hand tape
234.s: Johnston explains why she wants Gil's own account on tape rather than printed sources such as Feather's encyclopedia.
234.q: I know, but I didn't know it had any actual music in it.

234.t: Teaching himself to read and arrange from records and library scores
234.s: Gil says he is semi-literate at reading music. He learned arranging by copying records note for note and studying library scores.
234.q: I still can't read music too well, you know. I'm like what you call semi-literate in music. And I really never did practice reading music. I can write music for other people, to play you know. But to read other people's music, I'm not too quick at it.

96.t: The old Wolverines could not read music
96.s: Bix, the piano, drums and banjo couldn't read; all by ear.
96.q: Well this was in the old Wolverine band. The old Wolverines. This is 1924. And the piano player couldn't read and Bix didn't read very well. Or George Johnson the tenor saxophone player didn't read very well, hardly at all, just a little bit. And the drummer didn't read. And Bob Gillette, the banjo…

96.t: Today's musicians study; Eubie Blake on reading
96.s: Young musicians are better trained; Johnston relays Eubie Blake's story about the myth that Black musicians couldn't read.
96.q: : Well, they have the, fortunately they have the, we have talked about this for years. And they get the knowledge from us that the smartest thing to do is study and practice. And learn all your harmonies and where it is on your instrument. And if you play a different instrument, naturally piano has…

237.t: Tests of whether Black bands could read
237.s: Goodwin says doubters handed Black bands stock arrangements to test their reading.
237.q: Well, during this time you had people that were -- well you might say they were jazz buffs or whatever you might want to call them.

237.t: Begin the Beguine at the University Club for banker Kemper
237.s: Harlan Leonard's band sight-read a Latin chart for banker Kemper and Lovett's reading carried it.

124.t: Whether Black musicians could read music
124.s: McRae objects to the idea that Black musicians could not read, citing Armstrong, Jabbo Smith and Jenkins Orphanage graduates.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: It was a thing when they was trying to get black musicians on the staff. And they probably said I don't know if they can read.

124.s: He learned the saxophone parts by listening to records, reading well and following the lead alto.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: -- real carefully. Went along with the -- the main part I wanted to learn is with the saxophone. What the saxophone had to do, you know.

86.t: Reading and head arrangements in the early 1930s
86.s: Most of the playing was by ear and the written music was simple; Edison was building confidence as a soloist.
86.ch: Jeter-Pillars in Cleveland and St. Louis
86.q: Yeah, but most of it was from head, even in Alphonso Trent's band. Sy did a lot of writing in the band but it was near as complicated as the reading that you have to do nowadays. What we played in those days is like what beginners play to like what you have to play now in studios, you know.

86.t: Reading ability and head arrangements in the big bands

172.s: Silver Leaf read sheet music under Albert Batiste then Oscar Randall, with little ragtime.

250.t: The Queen Anne Room job at the Montleon

871.q: Would you call that a Dixieland band or a Reedin band or both? Well, it was a Reedin band. It was an orchestra. It was an orchestra.

761.t: SS Dixie trip and learning to read music
761.s: On the riverboat to New York he was found unable to read parts, which pushed him to take lessons; he also mentions working with Larry.

183.t: Alfred's story of the lights going out on the boat band
183.s: Alfred tells how the Piron boat band's players, who read only from music, could not play when the lights went out, naming those who could not play by ear.
183.ch: Learning trumpet and first bands in New Orleans
183.q: He said, now, didn't I tell you that? No, you can't play nothing. What happened, Gay? You can't play nothing. No, you see? The music automatically stopped.

A note, they never know. It's something for us hard, they don't know when they tune up. But if you train that ear,…

772.t: Piano lessons and learning to read music
772.s: He had lessons but argues reading only takes you so far; you pick out the melody and play it your way.

1023.t: Reading ability of Leon, Sharkey and the Hollywood sidemen
1023.s: Leon read better than Sharkey, who needed rehearsals. Pinero, the guitarist and the sax section are discussed as readers.
1023.q: Oh no, he, Sharky could read, but he, he was, he was a rehearsal reader, if you know what I mean. He'd have to rehearse a tune a few times to get it. But then, when, when we played the jazz tunes, Sharky would, uh, would run the brass section, you see.

256.s: He took one lesson, was told his ear was too good, and feared reading after Henny died.

He says, you can't learn to read music. You heard by hearsay. I took one lesson. And my brother Henny taught himself how to…

241.t: Reading with Desvigne versus faking with Kit Harris
241.s: Nelson contrasts the strict reading in Desvigne's band with the faking he learned from Kit Harris.
241.q: Well, I had to play this modern trombone, you know, read music and play sweet solos and arrangements.

184.t: Learning to read music from Jimmy Bertrand in Chicago
184.s: Tubby showed him how to hold sticks; he first learned to read notes in Chicago from Jimmy Bertrand.

568.s: Roy helped by encouraging rather than teaching; Hightower struggles to read, then buys the band white ducks and blue coats that impress white New Orleans.

Well, we went on with those numbers, like crip numbers that I played, until the band got so good, until Roy got to the place where he spent a little time with me. 662.t: Influences, repertoire and reading in the Celestin band
662.s: She had no particular influence. The band played popular music, then arranged music as a 14-piece reading band, and she improvised in solos.
662.q: Well, we played, when we first started out, it was popular music. And then when we went into a large band, which was 14 pieces, then we played only arrangements. Strictly reading, all reading musicians. It was wonderful. We had a lovely large band.

297.t: Trick wrong notes to test reading, and the Arban book
297.s: Gaspard planted wrong notes to see if he read or played by head; Interviewer compares Bunk's Arban book; Gaspard wrote solos.

266.t: Auditioning for Johnny Ronica's band after high school
266.s: Jones auditioned for the arranger Johnny Ronica at Lentz in the early 1950s but could not read well enough; Pat Sullivan was the lead trumpeter.

448.t: Bechet's effect on bands, his tunes, and not reading music
448.s: Bechet improved any group, wrote a Johnny Dodds tribute blues, and regretted weak reading.

181.t: Reading music and the country brass band teacher

271.t: Leonce's quick ear and listening to Black bands

619.t: Big Eye and Picou as music readers
619.s: Big Eye did not read music and Laurent helped him; Picou could read, though not brilliantly.

765.t: Playing verses; bands in front of the house
765.s: Playing verses with reading, and brass bands that bucked outside his house.

403.t: How Bolden differed from earlier reading bands
403.s: Earlier bands were all readers; Bolden could hear a piece and have his band playing it by daylight.
403.q: But Buddy Bowling, he could hear a band play, or hear music, and come with his band, get his band out with it, in between dances in the night, and before daylight he wanted, he played that piece he heard down there. Mm-hmm.

734.t: Learning to read music and his brothers' instruments

800.s: He describes reading treble clef on baritone, writing his own parts in the WPA band, and having printed music in the Navy.

675.s: Braud argues a musician who can read and fake gets work, and says Bechet had soul without reading.

1056.s: He only blew the horn after repairing a pad; he did not practice or read music, which struck others as strange.

1006.s: Johnny Dodds had a beautiful tone but did not read; Alexis won a roof garden job over Rene on his reading, unlike Louis Armstrong.

968.t: Previous owners of the banjo, instruction books and reading music
968.s: Frank Myers owned the banjo before; they look at Morris and McNeil method books, and Marrero says he plays mostly by ear and reads some.

880.t: Playing in the country band at Leclerc after 1913; reading and playing by head
880.s: Joseph returned to Leclerc in 1913 and played with the Holmes men, the only band there; they all read music and played by ear.

977.t: Reading music, learning from records, private parties

831.t: Learning to read music with Max Fink at the Lill Club
831.s: He learned to read by following parts as sousaphone player for Max Fink and ends with a Biloxi newspaper date for the photograph.
831.ch: Photographs, reading music and Wingy Manone

766.s: Wooden Joe could read, but bands then played by ear without orchestrations.

198.t: Who read music: Dodds, Charlie, Jimmie Noone
198.s: Barnes compares the reading ability of Bechet, Dodds, Blind Charlie and Noone, called Jimbo, and how loud and rough each was.

392.t: Reading music versus playing by ear
392.s: Raymond Burke, Harry Shields and George Lewis did not read; the cradle of jazz was not apparent to Sid.

306.t: George Lewis learns by ear; neighbours of the first Dixieland band

202.t: Earlier big bands, reading double stops, and tablature
202.s: He had played with Wald, Abe Lyman and Carl Hoff, brushed up his reading for Hoff's book, and objects to tablature; he also mentions current students.

And at that time I had to go and brush up on my reading because in Carl Hoff’s band, the violin player was the arranger. There was only one violin, but he wrote double stops for the guitar…

939.s: Brown notes Wes Montgomery could not read, and recalls Dizzy Gillespie telling her 'If you can hear it, you can sing it' before the Budokan, though she reads no music herself.
